The Anning barb, Gymnocypris firmispinatus, is a cyprinid endemic to the upper reaches of the Jinsha River basin, where it inhabits cold, fast-flowing montane streams. Field surveys indicate that newly hatched larvae emerge from demersal eggs at a wet weight of just 0.0041 grams [Wwb = 0.0041 grams], a mass derived from an egg diameter of approximately 1.98 millimeters. During their initial yolk-sac larval stage, these tiny prolarvae remain entirely lecithotrophic, relying on endogenous yolk reserves before transitioning to exogenous feeding. The species exhibits a distinct allometric shift during its larval-juvenile transition, with fin ray ossification and scale formation marking the onset of the juvenile period. Available data on growth trajectories suggest that G. firmispinatus follows a comparatively slow life-history pace relative to other schizothoracines, a pattern potentially linked to the oligotrophic, high-altitude environment it occupies. The prolonged early developmental phase is consistent with the energetic constraints imposed by cold water temperatures and seasonally limited prey availability in these headwater habitats.

Reproductive maturation in Gymnocypris firmispinatus occurs at a relatively modest body size; individuals typically attain puberty upon reaching a total length of 9 centimeters [Lp = 9 centimeters]. This threshold corresponds to the onset of gonad maturation and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, events that precede the first spawning event by a substantial interval. Field collections of gravid females indicate that the wet weight at which sexual maturation is achieved is approximately 5 grams [Wwp = approximately 5 grams], a value that reflects the modest somatic investment required before reproductive effort can begin. In contrast, the ultimate total length of the species, representing the maximum body size recorded in natural populations, reaches 24 centimeters [Li = 24 centimeters]. The corresponding ultimate wet weight has been documented at 149 grams [Wwi = 149 grams], a figure that underscores the considerable post-pubertal growth this fish can sustain. This substantial increase in body mass from the pubertal stage to the asymptotic size highlights the species' capacity for prolonged somatic expansion in its native environment.

Under a stable water temperature of 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the maximum reproductive output of Gymnocypris firmispinatus has been characterized through controlled laboratory trials that reflect the thermal regime of its natural habitat. At this temperature, mature females produce approximately 9 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 9 eggs per spawning event], and multiple spawning events occur throughout the extended breeding season, resulting in a sustained period of reproductive activity. This reproductive strategy is notable among schizothoracines, many of which exhibit lower fecundity due to the constraints of cold-water physiology. The energetic cost of such sustained oocyte production is considerable, requiring the mobilization of lipid reserves accumulated during the pre-spawning foraging period. The 23 °C thermal regime used in these trials is representative of the warmer summer temperatures in the species' downstream range, where most spawning activity is concentrated.

Longevity in Gymnocypris firmispinatus has been estimated from mark-recapture studies and examination of otolith microstructures. Under the thermal conditions typical of its native streams, maintained at approximately 23 °C [T = 23 °C], the maximum lifespan recorded is approximately 13 years [am = approximately 13 years], a duration that places G. firmispinatus among the longer-lived members of its genus. This trait is often associated with late maturity and iteroparous reproductive strategies in cold-water fishes, with the lifespan substantially exceeding that of many lowland cyprinids. The extended longevity reflects the slower metabolic pace and reduced predation pressure characteristic of high-elevation environments, where individuals from colder tributaries may exhibit slightly different longevity metrics due to reduced metabolic rates.

Comparative analyses across the Schizothoracinae reveal that Gymnocypris firmispinatus matures at a total length of 9 centimeters [Lp = 9 centimeters], a value intermediate within the genus. The pubertal wet weight of 5 grams [Wwp = 5 grams] is similarly positioned relative to congeneric species, reflecting a life-history trade-off between early reproduction and continued somatic growth. The ultimate body size of 24 centimeters [Li = 24 centimeters] and the associated asymptotic mass of 149 grams [Wwi = 149 grams] further illustrate this pattern, as individuals that delay maturation can achieve larger terminal sizes. The egg-derived neonatal wet weight of 0.0041 grams [Wwb = 0.0041 grams] is remarkably small, even by cyprinid standards, and necessitates a prolonged period of larval development before the onset of exogenous feeding. The combination of a sustained reproductive output with moderate fecundity per event and an extended lifespan of roughly 13 years [am = roughly 13 years] at 23 °C [T = 23 °C] collectively characterizes a species that invests in extended survival and moderate, iteroparous reproduction rather than a single intense spawning bout.
